title-group.article-title: Impact of concurrent chemotherapy dose on long-term survival in locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma: a 10-year single-center study

sec.title: Aims
sec.p: The aim of this study is to compare the acute adverse reactions and long-term efficacy of concurrent chemoradiotherapy with different doses of cisplatin in the treatment of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: One hundred forty patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated at a hospital in Guangxi, China from March to October 2010 were randomly assigned to the A group (n = 72) (80 mg/m ²) and a B group (n = 68) (100 mg/m ²) according to different cisplatin usage regimens. The acute toxicities and long-term survival of the two groups were compared and analyzed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The median follow-up time of this study was 125 months (5 -183 months), and the overall survival (OS), local recurrence-free survival (LRRFS), progression-free survival (PFS), and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) of the two groups were not statistically significant. The 10-year OS, LRRFS, PFS, and DMFS were 64.6%, 88.1%, 83.4%, and 97.7% in the B group and 66.5%, 90.8%, 84.5%, and 96.2% in the A group. Multivariate analysis showed that age and T stage were independent risk factors for DMFS. In term of acute toxicities, the control group had an increased risk of bone marrow suppression and renal dysfunction.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study shows that reducing the dose of cisplatin concomitant chemotherapy does not reduce the long-term survival benefit of patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and it is beneficial to reduce the risk of acute toxicities.
Keywords: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Concurrent chemoradiotherapy , Cisplatin , Dose intensity , Survival , Toxicity

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is one of the most common head and neck malignancies and demonstrates a remarkable regional aggregation, with the Guangxi region in China being an area of high incidence [1]. According to the latest guidelines, concurrent chemoradiotherapy is included as a Class I recommendation for locally advanced Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (LA-NPC) [2]. Platinum-based chemotherapy plays a pivotal role in the treatment of NPC [3]. In particular, the U.S. NCCN guidelines recommend cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy as the standard treatment for LA-NPC [4], as cisplatin can enhance the radiosensitivity of tumor cells during radiotherapy and improve local tumor control [5]. However, previous studies have shown that cisplatin-based concurrent chemotherapy increases the incidence of acute toxicities, thereby reducing patient compliance with treatment. In addition, studies have shown that [6] cisplatin exerts synergistic anti-tumor effects by inducing non-apoptotic cell death pathways such as ferroptosis. When tumors are sensitive enough to radiotherapy and related pathways induced by cisplatin, further increasing the dose of cisplatin may not enhance tumor killing, but instead increase the incidence of acute toxicity, thereby reducing patients’ compliance with treatment.

In recent years, some studies and reviews [7] have suggested that not all patients with LA-NPC derive additional benefit from increased conventional chemotherapy intensity. For certain patients, comparable tumor control can be achieved even with lower-intensity chemotherapy regimens. At present, the optimal dosage and frequency of concurrent chemotherapy remain a matter of debate in clinical practice [8, 9]. However, in the field of chemotherapy for LA-NPC, most studies have focused on optimizing induction chemotherapy regimens, while long-term survival outcomes related to concurrent chemotherapy dosing have been rarely reported. Given that the impact of concurrent chemotherapy dosage on long-term survival requires reliable evaluation after extended follow-up, we initiated the analysis once the long-term outcome data had become sufficiently mature. We conducted a single-center retrospective study of 140 patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma who received different doses of concurrent chemotherapy. The median follow-up time for this study was 10 years. This represents one of the longest follow-up cohorts in this context and provides valuable insights into the long-term effectiveness and safety of concurrent chemotherapy strategies in real-world clinical settings. Despite the single-center design and variability in adjuvant chemotherapy dosing, our study offers clinically relevant data that inform long-term prognosis and dosing considerations for the treatment of LA-NPC.

In recent years, the introduction of the “nasopharyngeal carcinoma ecology theory” has provided a novel conceptual framework for understanding NPC. This theory posits that NPC is a dynamic pathological ecosystem shaped by bidirectional interactions among tumor cells, stromal components, immune infiltrating cells, and microbiota. The theory offers mechanistic insights into treatment resistance and metastatic propensity, emphasizing the role of the tumor microenvironment in regulating therapeutic responses, and highlighting potential opportunities for microenvironment-targeted interventions. This ecological perspective enriches our understanding of the treatment challenges in NPC and underscores the importance of considering individualized approaches in therapy [10].

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: This study was a retrospective secondary analysis based on a previously conducted prospective cohort. The original study enrolled 160 patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma at a hospital in Guangxi between March and October 2010. According to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria of the present analysis, 20 patients with early-stage disease were excluded. Consequently, a total of 140 patients were included in the final analysis. In the initial prospective study, these patients were prospectively enrolled and randomly assigned to Group A (n = 68) or Group B (n = 72) using a random number table method. Treatment regimens and follow-up assessments were extracted from the original study and analyzed in accordance with the original protocol. All patients completed two cycles of concurrent chemotherapy. The average follow-up time of the study was 133 months, and the median follow-up time was 125 months (5-183 months). Five patients declined follow-up and did not complete the subsequent follow-up visits (Fig. 1). These five patients were included in the adverse reaction analysis but were excluded from the survival analysis. The characteristics of all patients are listed in (Table 1). The clinical baseline characteristics of patients in the two groups were balanced and comparable, with no significant statistical differences. This study was approved by the hospital’s ethics committee, with ethics approval number: KY2024559. Inclusion criteria: (1) Newly diagnosed nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients confirmed by biopsy and pathology; (2) Staging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma according to the 8th edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) / American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, classified as stage III to IV-A; (3) No prior antitumor treatment; (4) Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) score ≥ 80; (5) Normal liver and kidney function; (6) Age: 18 to 70 years. Exclusion criteria: (1) Patients with severe uncontrolled infections; (2) Patients with severe underlying medical conditions and/or those unable to tolerate chemotherapy; (3) Pregnant patients or those with other untreated malignancies; (4) Patients with concurrent other malignancies.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: All eligible patients received concurrent chemoradiotherapy with or without 2 to 3 cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy.

sec.title: Chemotherapy regimen
sec.p: Both groups received single-agent cisplatin as concurrent chemotherapy during radiotherapy according to their assigned regimens. The specific arrangements were as follows: 1. Hydration: After excluding contraindications to treatment, hydration was initiated 1–2 days before chemotherapy. 2.Antiemetic and supportive care: Antiemetic therapy, hepatoprotective and gastric mucosal protective agents, hydration and diuresis, as well as enhanced nutritional support were provided throughout chemotherapy. 3. Cisplatin dosing: In the B group, cisplatin was administered at 100 mg/m²/d1 or d1–3. In the A group, cisplatin was administered at 80 mg/m²/d1 or d1–3. The adjuvant chemotherapy regimen consisted of the PF protocol: cisplatin 80–100 mg/m²/d1 or d1–3 plus 5-fluorouracil 0.8–1.0 g/m²/ d1–5. Chemotherapy cycles and termination criteria: Both groups were scheduled to receive two cycles of concurrent chemotherapy unless treatment was delayed for more than one week due to hematologic toxicity, or more than two weeks due to non-hematologic toxicity. In such cases, patients were deemed intolerant to the regimen, and concurrent chemotherapy was discontinued.

In the original prospective trial, cisplatin at a dose of 100 mg/m² was administered as the standard regimen for concurrent chemoradiotherapy in patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. However, based on institutional clinical practice and considerations regarding tolerability and acute toxicity, the dose was reduced to 80 mg/m² in a subset of patients.This variation in dosing provided the rationale for the present retrospective analysis, enabling a comparison between the standard-dose group and the reduced-dose group in terms of long-term survival outcomes and safety profiles.

During the concurrent treatment phase, the planned cumulative cisplatin dose was 200 mg/m² (two cycles) in the 100 mg/m² group and 160 mg/m² in the 80 mg/m² group. Adjuvant chemotherapy consisted of 2–3 cycles of the PF regimen.Given the variability in the number of adjuvant chemotherapy cycles and the actual administered doses among patients, the total cumulative cisplatin dose throughout the entire treatment course was not completely uniform. The primary focus of the present study was the cisplatin dose intensity during the concurrent treatment phase.

sec.title: Radiotherapy regimen
sec.p: Patients in both groups received a radical radiotherapy regimen of Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) or conventional radiotherapy. All radiotherapy plans were discussed and decided by an expert group in the department, and radiotherapy was treated with Elekta linear accelerator. The radioactive source is 6MV-X ray and 9 ~ 12 MeV-electron ray.

list-item.p: Conventional radiotherapy implementation plan: (1) Immobilization and CT simulation: The patient lay in the supine position with an appropriately fitted headrest, the neck in a neutral position, and both shoulders relaxed and at the same height. The shoulders and upper back were in full contact with the treatment couch, with the arms positioned alongside the body and the legs kept together and extended. The patient’s midline was aligned with the longitudinal midline of the couch and the laser guidance system. A thermoplastic U-shaped mask was used to immobilize the head. Using an isocentric technique, the bilateral lateral opposing fields were defined on the simulator, and simulation radiographs were acquired for verification. (2) Based on the tumor extent determined by pre-treatment imaging, the target volumes were outlined on the simulation radiographs, and individualized lead blocks were fabricated by the mold workshop. (3) Radiation field design and dose distribution: In the first phase, lateral opposing faciocervical fields combined with an anterior lower-neck field were used, with a prescription dose of 36 Gy in 18 fractions. In the second phase, the spinal cord was avoided by switching to preauricular fields combined with an anterior whole-neck field, or to small faciocervical fields plus an anterior lower-neck field with an additional postauricular electron field. When necessary, supplementary fields—including skull base fields, ethmoid sinus fields, anterior nasal fields, and local electron boost fields to the neck—were applied. The total dose to the nasopharynx was 68–78 Gy, and the prophylactic dose to the neck was 54–56 Gy. Metastatic lymph nodes were boosted with 9–12 MeV β-electron beams to a total dose of 62–78 Gy at 2 Gy per fraction, once daily, five days per week. (4) During the first treatment session of each phase, verification images were obtained on the linear accelerator to ensure treatment accuracy and reproducibility.

IMRT implementation plan: (1) Immobilization: The patient was placed in the supine position on the flat immobilization board with an appropriately fitted headrest to maintain a comfortable posture. The shoulders were relaxed and kept at the same height, with the upper back in full contact with the board. Both arms were positioned alongside the body, and the legs were extended. The patient’s midline was aligned with the longitudinal midline of the board. A thermoplastic head–neck–shoulder mask was used for immobilization, and CT simulation was performed after the mask had cooled and hardened. (2) CT simulation: The same positioning was reproduced on the spiral CT simulator. The central reference plane was selected according to the IMRT irradiation range, and three-dimensional laser beams were used to mark reference points on the patient’s skin (anterior and bilateral). Crosshair markings with lead markers were placed on the thermoplastic mask. The scanning range extended from the vertex of the skull to the thoracic inlet, with a slice thickness of 2.5 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT images were then transferred to the treatment planning system. (3) Target delineation and Organs at Risk (OAR) contouring: The imaging data were transferred to the treatment planning system for three-dimensional reconstruction. Target volumes and normal organs were delineated by radiation oncologists. Tumor target delineation followed the principles outlined in ICRU Reports 50 and 62 [11, 12]. Tumor target volumes: GTVnx: The primary nasopharyngeal tumor as defined on contrast-enhanced CT and/or MRI, including the retropharyngeal lymph nodes. GTVnd: Cervical metastatic lymph nodes confirmed on contrast-enhanced CT and/or MRI, meeting at least one of the following criteria: short-axis diameter ≥ 1 cm; central necrosis; heterogeneous enhancement; nodal conglomeration; extracapsular extension; or clustered lymph nodes. Clinical target volumes (CTVs): CTV1: A 5–10 mm expansion from GTVnx, covering the soft tissues around the foramen lacerum, clivus base, sphenoid sinus floor, foramen ovale, the entire nasopharyngeal mucosa and a 0.5-cm submucosal layer, with posterior margin adjustments based on retropharyngeal lymph node involvement. CTV2: A 5–10 mm expansion from CTV1, including lymphatic regions containing GTVnd and prophylactic irradiation areas, delineated according to established contouring principles (e.g., clivus, petrous apex, pterygoid plates, parapharyngeal space, and cervical nodal levels II–V). Planning target volume (PTV): A uniform 3-mm margin was added to each target volume to generate the PTV, with appropriate margin reduction near critical organs-at-risk such as the spinal cord, brainstem, and optic nerves.

Organs-at-risk delineated: Parotid glands, spinal cord, brainstem, optic chiasm, optic nerves, pituitary gland, eyeballs, lenses, and others. (4) Treatment planning and evaluation: Prescription doses and dose constraints: PGTVnx: 68–78 Gy in 30–32 fractions; PGTVnd: 68–75 Gy in 30–32 fractions; PCTV1: 60–64 Gy in 30–32 fractions; PCTV2: 54–56 Gy in 30–32 fractions. OAR constraints: For example: brainstem ≤ 54 Gy; spinal cord ≤ 45 Gy; optic chiasm, optic nerves, and pituitary ≤ 50 Gy; temporal lobes 10–50 Gy; temporomandibular joints 30–50 Gy. Medical physicists designed and optimized coplanar nine-field inverse IMRT plans using the treatment planning system. All radiotherapy plans were reviewed by one to two associate chief physicians or chief physicians. Plan evaluation was performed based on dose–volume histograms (DVH) and isodose distribution. (5) Treatment delivery: After the treatment plan was approved, setup verification was performed, and radiotherapy was initiated once verification was confirmed.

sec.title: Follow up
sec.p: The objective of this study was to retrospectively evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated with different doses of concurrent chemotherapy, based on data derived from a previously conducted prospective randomized trial. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Secondary endpoints included local-regional recurrence-free survival (LRRFS), distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), progression-free survival (PFS), and the incidence of acute treatment-related adverse events. Follow-up was conducted through the medical records system and by phone, with follow-up content including the patient’s survival status, tumor progression, local regional recurrence, and distant metastasis. The final follow-up date for this study was March 31, 2025. Adverse reaction data were recorded and assessed within one month after concurrent chemotherapy. OS is defined as the time from the start of treatment to death from any cause. PFS is defined as the time from the start of treatment to the first disease progression or death from any cause. LRRFS is defined as the time to the first recurrence of nasopharyngeal and/or cervical region disease after treatment. DMFS is defined as the time from the start of treatment to the appearance of distant metastasis. For patients who experienced the first disease progression or death from any cause, the analysis of LRRFS was censored at the time of progression or death, and they were not included in subsequent local regional recurrence events.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were primarily performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). As this study represents a retrospective analysis of a fixed cohort comprising 140 patients derived from a previously conducted prospective randomized trial, no a priori sample size or statistical power calculation was performed.

Continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t-test, and categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square (χ²) test. Survival outcomes were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared between groups using the log-rank test. Multivariate analyses were conducted using the Cox proportional hazards regression model to assess the independent effects of covariates on survival outcomes.

Kaplan–Meier survival curves with numbers at risk were generated using R software (version 4.4.3) for graphical visualization. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Acute toxicity
sec.p: Table 2 shows the incidence of acute adverse in the two groups of patients. Among these, the occurrences of bone marrow suppression and renal function impairment are statistically significant (P < 0.05). In the B group, 40 patients (28.57%) experienced bone marrow suppression, while 33 patients (23.57%) in the A group experienced bone marrow suppression. Of these, 19 patients (13.57%) in the B group had grade III-IV bone marrow suppression, whereas only 9 patients (6.34%) in the A group had grade III-IV bone marrow suppression. Similarly, a higher proportion of renal function impairment was observed in the B group. Both groups experienced grade I-II renal function impairment, with 10 patients (7.14%) in the A group and 5 patients (5.37%) in the B group showing impaired renal function. These findings indicate an increased risk of bone marrow suppression and renal function impairment in the B group. Other adverse reactions, such as gastrointestinal reactions and liver function damage, did not show statistically significant differences between the two groups.

sec.title: Survival analysis
sec.p: Among the 135 patients who completed follow-up, 43 patients died, 12 had tumor progression, 21 had distant metastasis, and 6 had local regional recurrence. The 10-year LRRFS, PFS, DMFS, and OS for patients in the B group were 96.2%, 90.8%, 84.5%, and 66.5%, respectively, while in the A group they were 97.7%, 88.1%, 83.4%, and 64.6%, respectively. No statistically significant differences were found between the two groups (Fig. 2A, B, C, and D). Multivariable analysis showed that age and T stage were independent factors associated with DMFS (Table 3). Dose grouping was not an independent prognostic factor for any of the endpoints.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The NPC-0099 trial compared the efficacy of radiotherapy alone versus concurrent chemoradiotherapy in patients with locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The results demonstrated that the combined chemoradiotherapy group had significantly higher 3-year OS and PFS compared with the radiotherapy-alone group. Based on this landmark study, cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy has become the standard treatment for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma [13]. At present, advanced local tumor stage remains an independent risk factor for treatment failure, and distant metastasis is the predominant pattern of failure in LA-NPC [14].

Although induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (IC+CCRT) is currently the Class 1 recommended treatment for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, the addition of CCRT after induction chemotherapy significantly increases chemotherapy-related toxicities, particularly hematologic toxicity and gastrointestinal adverse effects [15]. For some elderly patients, those with poor physical condition, or those with multiple comorbidities, the high-intensity chemotherapy administered upfront may be poorly tolerated, often resulting in treatment interruptions or even discontinuation, which can ultimately compromise overall treatment outcomes.

For this patient population, it is necessary to balance treatment toxicity with survival benefits [16]. One strategy is to initiate concurrent chemoradiotherapy first and then determine subsequent treatment based on the patient’s tolerance. Cisplatin plays a radiosensitizing role in CCRT; however, its substantial toxicity poses a major chal-lenge in terms of safety management. High-dose cisplatin can reduce treatment compliance and quality of life [17]. A previous study [18] demonstrated that patients receiving cisplatin-containing regimens had a significantly higher incidence of grade III–IV hematologic and non-hematologic toxicities. Tang et al. [8] performed a statistical analysis of existing studies, including multiple cohort studies comparing weekly versus three-week cisplatin regimens. The results showed that there was no statistically significant difference between the two dosing regimens in 5-year OS, FFS, LRFS and DMFS. It is worth noting that in his study, it is known that the weekly regimen is more likely to have hematological adverse reactions, while the three-week regimen has more non-hematological adverse reactions. This suggests that adjusting dosing frequency has limited effect on long-term survival after reaching a certain dose threshold, whereas individualized dose adjustment can be used to improve tolerability. Historically, most studies have adopted a three-weekly regimen of cisplatin at 100 mg/m², which may provide good local control but is often associated with increased adverse events, potentially compromising overall treatment outcomes [19].

In the original prospective trials, the regimen of cisplatin 100 mg/m² every three weeks has been widely regarded as the standard for concurrent chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, based on evidence from previous randomized controlled studies demonstrating a survival benefit of chemoradiotherapy. However, in real world clinical practice, dose-reduction strategies for cisplatin have been adopted in some patients with risks of myelosuppression or renal impairment. In recent years, oncological research has increasingly recognized that once a certain dose threshold is reached, further escalation of cytotoxic drug doses does not necessarily confer a proportional survival benefit. Most available literature has focused on short-term or intermediate-term follow-up [20, 21]. Although such data provide useful insights into treatment efficacy, they may be insufficient for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. A 5-year observation window may fail to capture long-term disease progression and patient reported outcomes. In the same prospective cohort, two chemotherapy dose levels were implemented, providing a valuable opportunity for this long-term retrospective analysis. By comparing the standard-dose and reduced-dose groups, we sought to evaluate whether moderate dose reduction compromises long-term survival while potentially improving safety. With intensity-modulated radiotherapy markedly enhancing local control in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and systemic treatment strategies continuously evolving, the necessity of maintaining full-dose cisplatin for all patients remains to be determined. Therefore, we aimed to collect a retrospective dataset spanning 10 years to investigate the efficacy and toxicity differences between different cisplatin doses during concurrent chemoradiotherapy, evaluate long-term survival outcomes in both groups, and identify relevant prognostic factors, thereby contributing long-term follow-up evidence for patients with nasopharyngeal carcinom. This study provides unique long-term survival data for LA-NPC patients who received different doses of concurrent chemotherapy. Compared with most published studies with a follow-up of 3–5 years, our dataset offers a rare opportunity to evaluate late survival patterns and the durability of treatment effects. Although the study is limited by its single center design and a moderate sample size of 140 patients, these factors also ensure consistency in treatment protocols and follow-up management. The heterogeneity in adjuvant chemotherapy administration reflects real-world clinical practice and highlights the feasibility of various dosing strategies. Overall, our findings contribute to understanding the long-term impact of concurrent chemotherapy dose on survival outcomes and may serve as a reference for future prospective studies or multi-center collaborations.

Previously, a phase II clinical trial [22] conducted by Japanese researchers demonstrated that a dose of 80 mg/m² was effective and feasible for treating Asian patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma. In our study, no statistically significant differences were observed between the experimental and control groups in LRRFS, PFS, DMFS, or OS, indicating that the survival outcomes of the low-dose group were not inferior to those of the high-dose group. Prior studies have also reported that the 2-year distant metastasis-free survival and recurrence-free survival rates did not differ significantly between the low-dose (80 mg/m²) and high-dose (100 mg/m²) groups [23], which is consistent with our findings. This may be related to the inherent radiosensitivity and chemosensitivity of nasopharyngeal carcinoma [24]. For LA-NPC, radiotherapy serves as the primary curative modality, while the main roles of concurrent chemotherapy are to enhance tumor radiosensitivity and eradicate micrometastases [25]. It is possible that the radiosensitizing effect of cisplatin reaches a plateau, such that increasing the dose provides limited additional benefit and thus fails to produce statistically significant improvements.

In this study, the incidences of bone marrow suppression and renal impairment differed significantly between the two groups, indicating that patients receiving the high-dose regimen had an increased risk of bone marrow suppression and kidney dysfunction. Although patient survival remains the primary endpoint, the impact of treatment-related adverse effects on quality of life should not be overlooked, as cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity can lead to long-term health risks [26].

When interpreting the results of this study, it is important to distinguish between “cumulative cisplatin exposure” and “dose intensity during the concurrent phase.” In the concurrent treatment phase, the planned cumulative doses were 200 mg/m² for the 100 mg/m² group and 160 mg/m² for the 80 mg/m² group. In our study, actual cumulative doses exhibited some variability, reflecting individualized clinical considerations such as renal function, treatment tolerance, and comorbidities. Most patients received 2–3 cycles of PF adjuvant chemotherapy after completing concurrent chemoradiotherapy, resulting in inter-patient variation in total cisplatin exposure over the entire treatment course. These variations do not indicate protocol deviations, but rather reflect real world clinical practice and provide insights into feasible dosing strategies. Therefore, this study primarily reflects differences in dose intensity during the concurrent treatment phase, rather than the absolute cumulative cisplatin dose over the entire treatment course. From both a radiobiological and clinical perspective, the concurrent phase may represent a critical window during which cisplatin exerts its radiosensitizing effects, potentially exerting a greater impact on locoregional control than subsequent adjuvant therapy.

In recent years, concerns regarding the tolerability and toxicity burden of concurrent chemotherapy have driven the development of individualized dosing strategies in both domestic and international studies [27]. Although the classic concurrent cisplatin regimen improves local control rates, its acute toxicities can affect treatment compliance in real-world settings, particularly among older patients or those with poor nutritional status. Such adverse effects prevent some patients from completing the standard dose, creating an urgent clinical need to explore more individualized and better-tolerated concurrent treatment strategies. Meanwhile, immunotherapy (ICIs) has rapidly advanced in the management of locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, offering a new direction for chemotherapy dose individualization. Immune-related adverse events generally occur less frequently than cisplatin-related toxicities [28]. Several studies have shown that [29, 30] combining immune checkpoint inhibitors with radiotherapy or with attenuated concurrent chemotherapy can maintain tumor control while providing a more manageable toxicity profile. Against this background, the variability in concurrent chemotherapy doses observed in our study did not substantially compromise long-term survival, suggesting that dose reduction may be an acceptable strategy for selected low-risk or less-tolerant patients. With the continued development of immunotherapy, a more refined treatment paradigm may emerge—one that tailors concurrent chemotherapy dosing based on tumor biology, response to induction chemotherapy, toxicity risk, and patient preference, and even partially replaces chemotherapy intensity with immunotherapy in certain patient subgroups.

This study was conducted after a median follow-up of 10 years, allowing for a more robust and clinically meaningful assessment of overall survival and disease control. The timing of this analysis reflects the inherent need for long-term follow-up to address the research question.

This study has several limitations. First, as the data were derived from a single center with a relatively small sample size, the findings may lack regional representativeness. Second, given the long follow-up period, some degree of loss to follow-up was inevitable. Such missing data associated with prolonged follow-up may introduce selection bias. Third, most patients in this study received adjuvant chemotherapy, and adjuvant treatment information was partially incomplete. This may, to some extent, attenuate the “pure effect” of concurrent chemotherapy dose on long-term survival outcomes. Although our baseline comparison showed no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment may still act as a potential confounder. Future studies with more standardized adjuvant chemotherapy protocols or prospective designs that better control adjuvant treatment are warranted to further validate our findings.

In summary, based on 10-year follow-up results, this study demonstrates that low-dose concurrent chemotherapy provides long-term survival outcomes comparable to those of the conventional-dose regimen in patients with LA-NPC. Although the use of adjuvant chemotherapy was not completely uniform, multivariable adjustments indicated that the concurrent chemotherapy dose was not an independent predictor of long-term overall survival. These findings suggest that dose optimization of concurrent chemotherapy may be feasible for patients with poor treatment tolerance or comorbidities. Further validation through multicenter, prospective studies is warranted.
